numbers.sentence: Experimental results on wide residual networks show that this leads to consistent gains, yielding even new state-of-the-art results ( , 16-layer-deep wide residual network with dropout achieves 1.64% error on SVHN).

We show indicative results in table , where in this case we took WRN-40-2 with convolutions and trained several networks with different deepening factor , same number of parameters (2.2 ) and same number of convolutional layers.
Yet, it is interesting that these networks have comparable number of parameters, 8.9 and 10.2 , suggesting that depth does not add regularization effects compared to width at this level.

Also, wide WRN-28-10 outperforms thin ResNet-1001 by 0.92% (with the same minibatch size during training) on CIFAR-10 and 3.46% on CIFAR-100, having 36 times less layers (see table ).
Also, wide WRN-28-10 outperforms thin ResNet-1001 by 0.92% (with the same minibatch size during training) on CIFAR-10 and 3.46% on CIFAR-100, having 36 times less layers (see table ).

We note that the result of 4.64% with ResNet-1001 was obtained with batch size 64, whereas we use a batch size 128 in all of our experiments (i.e., all other results reported in table are with batch size 128).

In general, we observed that CIFAR mean/std preprocessing allows training wider and deeper networks with better accuracy, and achieved 18.3% on CIFAR-100 using WRN-40-10 with parameters (table ), giving a total improvement of 4.4% over ResNet-1001 and establishing a new state-of-the-art result on this dataset.

In general, we observed that CIFAR mean/std preprocessing allows training wider and deeper networks with better accuracy, and achieved 18.3% on CIFAR-100 using WRN-40-10 with parameters (table ), giving a total improvement of 4.4% over ResNet-1001 and establishing a new state-of-the-art result on this dataset.
We used cross-validation to determine dropout probability values, 0.3 on CIFAR and 0.4 on SVHN.
We used cross-validation to determine dropout probability values, 0.3 on CIFAR and 0.4 on SVHN.

Dropout decreases test error on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 by 0.11% and 0.4% correnspondingly (over median of 5 runs and mean/std preprocessing) with WRN-28-10, and gives improvements with other ResNets as well (table ).

Dropout decreases test error on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 by 0.11% and 0.4% correnspondingly (over median of 5 runs and mean/std preprocessing) with WRN-28-10, and gives improvements with other ResNets as well (table ).
To our knowledge, that was the first result to approach 20% error on CIFAR-100, even outperforming methods with heavy data augmentation.
We additionally trained WRN-16-8 with dropout on SVHN (table ), which achieves 1.54% on SVHN - the best published result to our knowledge.
Without dropout it achieves 1.81%.

In the rest of the paper we use the following notation: WRN- - denotes a residual network that has a total number of convolutional layers and a widening factor (for example, network with 40 layers and times wider than original would be denoted as WRN-40-2).
For ImageNet, we find that using pre-activation in networks with less than 100 layers does not make any significant difference and so we decide to use the original ResNet architecture in this case.
As can be seen, all networks with 40, 22 and 16 layers see consistent gains when width is increased by 1 to 12 times.
It is however clear that it is unnecessary to have residual networks with more than 50 layers due to computational reasons.
Despite having only 34 layers, this model achieves state-of-the-art single model performance, outperforming even ResNet-152 and Inception-v4-based models.

We demonstrate that wide networks with only 16 layers can significantly outperform 1000-layer deep networks on CIFAR, as well as that 50-layer outperform 152-layer on ImageNet, thus showing that the main power of residual networks is in residual blocks, and not in extreme depth as claimed earlier.
